focus: Bayes' rule for a diagnostic test: how prevalence (prior), sensitivity and specificity determine the positive predictive value P(disease | positive test). Let the learner change the three probabilities. Show the counts in a population of 1000 (true positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives) and the resulting posterior. Guide them through a rare disease with a good test (low PPV) and a common disease. Check that PPV equals prevalence when sensitivity + specificity = 1 (an uninformative test) and that PPV = 1 when specificity = 1 and sensitivity > 0.
audience: Engineering undergraduates with basic probability who have not seen diagnostic testing.
excerpt: (paraphrased) Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive, and specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative. Neither tells a clinician the probability that a particular patient with a positive result actually has the disease. That probability, the positive predictive value (PPV), is the proportion of positive test results that are true positives. Unlike sensitivity and specificity, predictive values depend on the prevalence of the disease in the population being tested: PPV = (sensitivity x prevalence) / (sensitivity x prevalence + (1 - specificity) x (1 - prevalence)). When the disease is rare, even a test with high sensitivity and specificity can yield a low positive predictive value, because false positives from the large healthy group outnumber the true positives. The negative predictive value (NPV) is the proportion of negative results that are true negatives.
